sources.note: Read 2026-11-17 through a summarizing fetch. Success rate, the share of users who complete a target task, is 'the bottom line of usability'; it is coarse and says nothing about why users fail; small qualitative tests give design insight, not tight intervals; partial success can be reported in labeled levels, not averaged as numbers.

sources.note: Read 2026-11-17 through a summarizing fetch. In a thinking-aloud test 'you ask test participants to use the system while continuously thinking out loud'; 'a handful of users' gives the most important insights; facilitator prompts can change behavior.

brief.situation: You ran a think-aloud usability test of the new booking flow at Brookfield Dental Group (fictional) with five participants and one task: book a cleaning next week. The product owner reads the satisfaction scores as a pass. Release is at 16:00. It is 15:05. The test data uses invented participants and no patient records.
handover: You have recordings, notes, completion and time for each participant.
A quick design fix and a 5-person retest fit in the hour.
howItWorks: Pick a step from the action list: look, change, check or ship. Nothing you pick is typed or executed: every step shows an authored result.
Each step takes working minutes, and the clock moves by the minutes it takes. The deadline runs on the same clock.
Shipping is final for this case. Afterwards you record what you found and explain your reasoning.

scoring.modelReasoning: Satisfaction of 4.1 measures liking; the task measure is success, and only 2 of 5 booked, at more than twice the target time. Think-aloud notes put every failure at one point: after picking a time, the gray Continue button looks disabled. That is a design problem, not a user problem. Make Continue look active with feedback on selection and retest with five new participants on the same task. A tooltip guesses; emailing instructions blames users.
